items.title: Some Versus All
items.question: A claim says some students passed. A listener concludes that some students failed. What is the error?
choices: The claim says nothing at all
items.correctExplanation: Right. 'Some passed' leaves open the possibility that every last one passed.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is some does not mean all. The word some guarantees at least one, not that any were left out.
items.lessonContent:
Quantifiers carry exact logical force.
Some guarantees at least one, nothing more.
Do not read an exclusion into a partial claim.
Check what a statement actually rules out.
Share this: restate one everyday claim in strict logical terms.

items.title: Existence Question
items.question: A rule says all trespassers will be prosecuted. Does the rule have to be triggered at least once?
choices: All requires at least one case
items.correctExplanation: Right. A universal rule can stand even if no case ever satisfies its condition.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is all does not imply existence. The statement constrains members of a set without asserting that the set is non-empty.
items.lessonContent:
Universals constrain without guaranteeing cases.
Rules can be true yet never triggered.
Separate the condition from its instances.
Ask what a statement asserts exists.
Share this: find one rule that has never needed to apply.

items.title: Middle Term
items.question: Two premises in a syllogism never share a common term. What must be added for a valid conclusion?
choices: The middle term must be linked
items.correctAnswer: The middle term must be linked
items.correctExplanation: Right. A shared middle term is what connects the subject of one premise to the predicate of the other.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the middle term must be linked. Without that bridge, two true premises cannot yield a conclusion about a third thing.
items.lessonContent:
Syllogisms rely on a connecting term.
No shared term means no reliable link.
Structure decides whether a conclusion follows.
Look for the bridge between premises.
Share this: identify the connecting term in one argument you use.

items.title: Overlapping Circles
items.question: In a Venn diagram, two circles overlap. What does the shared region represent?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Anything inside both circles belongs to each of the two groups at once.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is overlapping circles show shared members. The overlap is the intersection, the things both sets contain.
items.lessonContent:
Diagrams make set relations visible.
Overlap marks shared membership.
Draw before arguing about groups.
Pictures expose hidden assumptions.
Share this: sketch two overlapping groups to test a claim.

items.title: No Shared Members
items.question: Two categories have no members in common at all. What are they called?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Disjoint groups never overlap, so nothing can belong to both.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is disjoint sets share no members. Their circles on a diagram do not touch, which is a strong logical constraint.
items.lessonContent:
Some groups exclude each other entirely.
Naming the relation clarifies reasoning.
Exclusion can be tested case by case.
Draw the boundary before arguing.
Share this: find two categories that cannot both apply.

items.title: Nested Sets
items.question: Every member of one group is also a member of a larger group. How is the smaller group described?
choices: A subset lies entirely within another
items.correctAnswer: A subset lies entirely within another
items.correctExplanation: Right. A subset sits wholly inside a larger set without anything outside it.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a subset lies entirely within another. Confusing subset with superset reverses the direction of containment.
items.lessonContent:
Containment has a direction.
Subset and superset are not interchangeable.
State which is inside which.
Test membership to confirm the relation.
Share this: name one group that fits entirely inside another.

items.title: Outside the Set
items.question: What is the set of everything not included in a given group called?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The complement contains every element outside the original set, relative to a universe.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is complement means everything outside. It depends on what universe of things you are considering, so context matters.
items.lessonContent:
Negation has a scope.
The outside depends on the universe chosen.
Define the frame before using complements.
Ambiguity hides in unstated universes.
Share this: state the frame for one claim about what is outside.

items.title: Negating All
items.question: What is the correct negation of the statement 'all birds fly'?
items.correctExplanation: Right. One counterexample suffices, so the negation is that at least one bird does not fly.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is negating all gives some not. 'No birds fly' is far too strong and does not follow from a single exception.
items.lessonContent:
Negation uses the minimum counterexample.
One exception refutes a universal.
Do not overshoot in the opposite direction.
Test a negation against a single case.
Share this: negate one sweeping claim with the weakest counterexample.

items.title: Negating Some
items.question: What is the correct negation of 'some people are left-handed'?
items.correctExplanation: Right. To deny that at least one exists, you must claim there are none at all.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is negating some gives none. The opposite of 'at least one' is 'not even one', not merely 'not all'.
items.lessonContent:
Existence claims negate to absence.
At least one opposes none at all.
Match the strength of the denial.
Avoid confusing contrary and contradictory.
Share this: write the exact denial of one existence claim.

items.title: Combined Groups
items.question: What operation collects every element that belongs to either of two groups, including the overlap?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The union gathers all members of both, counting the shared region only once.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is union combines both groups. Intersection is the opposite move, keeping only what both share.
items.lessonContent:
Union gathers, intersection narrows.
Two operations mirror and and or.
Name the operation before computing.
Overlap is counted once in a union.
Share this: decide whether a question calls for combining or narrowing.

items.title: Common Members
items.question: What operation keeps only the elements shared by two groups?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The intersection is exactly the overlap between the two sets.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is intersection contains common members. It answers which things satisfy both conditions at once.
items.lessonContent:
Intersection answers both-at-once questions.
It can be empty when groups are disjoint.
Narrowing reveals precise categories.
Check the overlap before concluding.
Share this: find what two of your commitments have in common.

items.title: Universal Affirmative
items.question: How is the proposition 'all S are P' classified in traditional logic?
choices: The universal affirmative states all S are P
The particular negative denies some S
The universal negative denies all S
The particular affirmative notes some S
items.correctAnswer: The universal affirmative states all S are P
items.correctExplanation: Right. It is universal in quantity and affirmative in quality, embracing the whole subject class.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the universal affirmative states all S are P. Its quantity is universal and its quality affirmative.
items.lessonContent:
Propositions have quantity and quality.
Universal covers all; particular covers some.
Affirmative joins; negative separates.
Classify before reasoning.
Share this: classify one claim by its quantity and quality.

items.title: Particular Negative
items.question: Which description fits the statement 'some S are not P'?
choices: The particular negative states some S are not P
The universal negative denies all S
The universal affirmative includes all S
The particular affirmative notes some S
items.correctAnswer: The particular negative states some S are not P
items.correctExplanation: Right. It is particular in quantity, since it concerns some, and negative in quality.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the particular negative states some S are not P. The word some fixes the quantity while not fixes the quality.
items.lessonContent:
Small words set logical classification.
Some marks particular scope.
Not marks negative quality.
Classify precisely before arguing.
Share this: rewrite one sentence into formal logical form.

items.title: Shared Term Rule
items.question: Two premises about entirely unrelated subjects cannot yield a conclusion about them. What is missing?
choices: A valid syllogism needs a shared term
A valid syllogism needs longer premises
A valid syllogism needs a negative
A valid syllogism needs three subjects
items.correctAnswer: A valid syllogism needs a shared term
items.correctExplanation: Right. The shared term is the bridge that lets a third claim follow.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a valid syllogism needs a shared term. Without a common term, the premises float free of each other.
items.lessonContent:
Bridges connect premises.
No common term means no link.
Structure, not truth, drives validity.
Find the term the premises share.
Share this: check the bridge in one argument you hear today.

items.title: Double Negative
items.question: What is wrong with a syllogism whose two premises are both negative?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Two exclusions cancel into no connection, so no affirmative link survives.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is two negatives cannot conclude positively. Since both premises deny, nothing is joined to support a positive claim.
items.lessonContent:
Two denials leave nothing connected.
Validity depends on the form.
Check whether premises build a link.
Rewrite negatives to see the gap.
Share this: spot one argument that only states what is not.

items.title: Middle Undistributed
items.question: A syllogism's shared term is never applied to all its members. Which fallacy results?
choices: An undistributed middle is a fallacy
A distributed middle is a fallacy
items.correctAnswer: An undistributed middle is a fallacy
items.correctExplanation: Right. If the bridge term never covers its whole class, the link can slip past the intended overlap.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is an undistributed middle is a fallacy. The premises may be true while the connection between them is accidental.
items.lessonContent:
Shared terms must cover their range.
Partial links can mislead.
True premises do not save a broken form.
Check how much of the middle is used.
Share this: test whether a shared term is used fully.

items.title: Illicit Terms
items.question: A conclusion claims more about a term than the premises support. What is the violation?
items.correctExplanation: Right. A valid conclusion cannot assert something the premises never established about a term.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is an illicit term breaks validity. The conclusion overreaches what the premises licensed.
items.lessonContent:
Conclusions cannot exceed their premises.
Every term must be earned.
Check scope before accepting a result.
Spot overreach by comparing claims.
Share this: find one conclusion that says more than its evidence.

items.title: Quantity and Quality
items.question: What two features together define the type of a categorical proposition?
choices: Quantity and quality define a proposition
Length and clarity define a proposition
Speaker and audience define a proposition
Tense and mood define a proposition
items.correctAnswer: Quantity and quality define a proposition
items.correctExplanation: Right. Whether it concerns all or some, and whether it affirms or denies, fixes its logical type.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is quantity and quality define a proposition. These two axes generate the four classic forms.
items.lessonContent:
Two axes classify categorical claims.
Quantity: all or some.
Quality: affirm or deny.
Classify first, then reason.
Share this: label one claim as all or some, and affirm or deny.

items.title: Diagram Test
items.question: How can you quickly test whether a categorical argument's form is valid?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Drawing the premises and checking whether the conclusion is forced makes form visible.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is Venn diagrams test validity visually. If some arrangement satisfies the premises yet violates the conclusion, the form is invalid.
items.lessonContent:
Visual tools expose logical form.
Draw premises, then look for counterexamples.
One valid arrangement is not enough.
A diagram can show what must follow.
Share this: sketch one argument instead of arguing it aloud.

items.title: Chain of Alls
items.question: If all A are B and all B are C, what follows about A and C?
choices: Nothing follows about A and C
items.correctExplanation: Right. Universal inclusion chains, so every A is also a C.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is chained universal statements transfer. Inclusion is transitive when the middle term is distributed throughout.
items.lessonContent:
Inclusion can be transitive.
Chains require full coverage at each step.
Direction matters: the reverse does not follow.
Follow the links from start to finish.
Share this: trace one chain of inclusions to its end.

items.title: One Way Some
items.question: From 'some A are B', what can you correctly conclude about B?
choices: Some A are B does not reverse cleanly
items.correctAnswer: Some A are B does not reverse cleanly
items.correctExplanation: Right. The statement guarantees an overlap, but reversing it without care can overstate the claim.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is some A are B does not reverse cleanly. At most you may infer that some B are A, never a universal claim.
items.lessonContent:
Converse inferences are risky.
Particular statements reverse only weakly.
Do not upgrade some into all.
State exactly what an overlap licenses.
Share this: check the converse of one claim before using it.

items.title: Enough Condition
items.question: What is a condition that is enough on its own to bring about an outcome?
choices: A sufficient condition guarantees the outcome
items.correctAnswer: A sufficient condition guarantees the outcome
items.correctExplanation: Right. If the condition holds, the outcome must follow, without needing anything else.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a sufficient condition guarantees the outcome. It may not be the only route, but it is always enough.
items.lessonContent:
Conditions differ in strength.
Sufficient means enough by itself.
Necessary means required but perhaps not enough.
Name which kind a claim involves.
Share this: classify one condition in a rule you follow.

items.title: Required Condition
items.question: What is a condition that must hold for an outcome, though it may not be enough alone?
choices: A necessary condition is required but not enough
A sufficient condition is always enough
items.correctAnswer: A necessary condition is required but not enough
items.correctExplanation: Right. Without it the outcome cannot occur, yet its presence does not guarantee the outcome.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a necessary condition is required but not enough. Confusing it with sufficiency leads to the converse error.
items.lessonContent:
Necessary means cannot do without.
It need not guarantee the result.
Separate requirement from guarantee.
Test by removing the condition.
Share this: identify one requirement that is not a guarantee.

items.title: Denied Antecedent
items.question: From 'if it rains, the ground is wet' someone concludes that because it did not rain, the ground is dry. What fallacy is this?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The ground could be wet for many other reasons, so the absence of rain proves nothing.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is denying the antecedent is invalid. Other causes can produce the same outcome, so the denial does not follow.
items.lessonContent:
One cause is not the only cause.
Absence of a trigger does not remove the effect.
Conditionals license only some inferences.
List rival causes before concluding.
Share this: name an alternative cause for one effect you assume.

items.title: Affirming the Consequent
items.question: Given that rain makes the ground wet, what is wrong with arguing that a wet ground proves it rained?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Other causes could wet the ground, so the effect does not prove that particular cause.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is affirming the consequent is invalid. The valid move is to deny the consequent, not to affirm it.
items.lessonContent:
Effects can have several causes.
Inferring one cause from an effect is unsafe.
The valid conditional move denies the consequent.
Look for other explanations first.
Share this: find one effect you blamed on a single cause.
